# The Private Credit Panic: Why Wall Street’s Big Winners are Now Losing | Real Eisman Playbook Ep 33

First listed: 2025-11-10 | Evaluation cutoff: 2026-11-10

[Back to library](../README.md)

## Source versions

- [YouTube: The Private Credit Panic: Why Wall Street’s Big Winners are Now Losing | Real Eisman Playbook Ep 33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2rZ3UXbRvoI) - 2025-11-10
- [Substack: The Private Credit Panic: Why Wall Street’s Big Winners are Now Losing | Real Eisman Playbook Ep 33](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/the-private-credit-panic-why-wall-3e8) - 2025-11-10

Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

## Summary

Glenn Schorr and Eisman distinguish operating businesses from stock valuations across private markets, banks and traditional asset managers. Durable funding, delayed exits, securities runoff and fee pressure offer useful mechanisms. Private-credit reassurance is incomplete: public versus private financing was not a clean distinction in First Brands, and tight public spreads do not logically rule out private-manager weakness. Citi and QQQ illustrate subsequent operational progress without settling every valuation claim.

Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.

- [Banking system conditions, June 2026 supervision report](https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2026-june-supervision-and-regulation-report-report-banking-system-conditions.htm) (2026-06-11): Q1 nonperforming-loan, loan-loss and reserve ratios declined slightly at most large banks. - [FSB warns on private-credit vulnerabilities](https://www.fsb.org/2026/05/fsb-warns-on-private-credit-vulnerabilities/) (2026-05-06): Identifies opaque valuations, lower-quality leveraged borrowers, sector concentration, layered leverage and bank/insurer linkages; notes rising PIK and some defaults. Report emphasizes data gaps and does not predict a completed systemic crisis.

## Framework and tools

- Separate manager equity valuation from credit-portfolio marks and borrower defaults.
- Match asset and liability duration without ignoring surrender, leverage and credit risk.
- Measure private-equity returns using timing as well as money multiples.
- A past mistake can create a forward earnings recovery opportunity at the right price.
- Normalize ROE versus RoTCE before comparing banks.
- Distinguish settlement technology from underlying asset risk.
- Model AUM, flows and fee rates separately.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- Private versus public credit composition
- MOIC and holding-period annualization
- Insurance asset-liability duration
- Bank securities yield runoff
- ROE and RoTCE denominators
- AUM flow and fee-rate bridge
- Token settlement and retained risks

## Source cautions

Steve Eisman interviews Evercore analyst Glenn Schorr. Host restatements are separately recorded where he adopts a substantive proposition.
- All 1737caption lines were read.
- The interview explicitly identifies recording on November 3, 2025, ahead of Apollo's November 4 report; publication was November 10.
- Opening montage repeats the interview.
- Contemporaneous stock declines are not prospective price targets.
- Guest recommendations and guest revision about Fraser are separate from Eisman views.
- Claims about fraud or scandals are not treated as adjudicated findings.
